extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners evaluating U.S. patent subject-matter eligibility (35 U.S.C. §101)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing whether claim additional elements amount to an 'inventive concept' or 'significantly more' than a judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature) under U.S. case law and USPTO interim guidance. Helps determine what claim limitations qualify as sufficiently transformative/meaningful versus those that do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to the functioning of a computer itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that improve how a computer operates (e.g., reduced memory use, faster computation, improved output quality) can qualify as 'significantly more' than a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: RCT v. Microsoft — a halftoning process that generated a mask, compared pixels, and used comparison results to convert a binary image to a halftoned image; the process used less memory, had faster computation time, and produced improved image quality compared to other masks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to another technology or technical field
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that improve a technology or technical field (outside general-purpose computing) can be 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Diamond v. Diehr — use of the Arrhenius equation to improve rubber-molding process control; SiRF Technology v. ITC — GPS receiver software using a mathematical formula to improve position determination in weak-signal environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying the judicial exception with, or by use of, a particular machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting application of the judicial exception by a particular, specially claimed machine (with specific structural/functional details) can demonstrate 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mackay Radio & Telegraph v. Radio Corp. of America — a mathematical formula employed using a particular type of antenna with details such as shape, conductors, length, and angle. Note: a general-purpose computer that applies a judicial exception using conventional computer functions has not been found to qualify as a particular machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimed processes that transform a particular article into a different state or thing can supply 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Tilghman v. Proctor — subjecting a fat-and-water mixture to heat with parameters, resulting in transformation of fatty bodies into fatty acids and glycerine. Note: the mere manipulation or reorganization of data does not satisfy the transformation prong (see Cybersource Corp. v. Retail Decisions, Inc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting specific, unconventional limitations or steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activity) can be 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: DDR Holdings, LLC v. Hotels.com, L.P. — claims recited automatic identification of a host web page, retrieval of 'look and feel' information, and generation of a hybrid web page combining merchant information with host look-and-feel, which differed from conventional hyperlink behavior and amounted to significantly more than an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking to a technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that do more than generally tie a judicial exception to a technology—i.e., meaningful concrete steps or structure—can constitute 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Diamond v. Diehr — beyond the Arrhenius equation, the claim recited installing rubber in a press, closing the mold, constantly measuring temperature, recalculating cure time, and opening the press at the proper time; these meaningful limitations limited the claim to practical application and were not an attempt to patent the mathematical equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding the words 'apply it' or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer (insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply appending language directing application of a judicial exception on a computer or giving high-level implementation instructions does not supply 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank — recitation of intermediated settlement as performed by a generic computer amounted to mere instructions to apply the abstract idea; Gottschalk v. Benson — converting BCD to binary had no substantial practical application except with a computer, merely stating the judicial exception while adding words to 'apply it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Appending well-understood, routine and conventional activities specified at a high level (insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding conventional industry activities, recited at a high level of generality, does not convert a judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mayo v. Prometheus — claim recited a natural correlation plus instructing a doctor to measure metabolite levels 'using any known process'; Alice Corp. — requiring a generic computer to perform routine functions (creating/maintaining shadow accounts, obtaining data, adjusting balances, issuing automated instructions) was insufficient because those were well-understood, routine, conventional activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception (insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconsequential pre- or post-solution activities (mere data gathering, consulting/updating logs, user requests) do not add 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ultramercial, Inc. v. Hulu, Inc. — steps of consulting/updating an activity log, requiring a user request, and restricting public access added nothing of practical significance; Cybersource Corp. v. Retail Decisions — obtaining transaction information via the Internet was mere data gathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally linking the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that only generally tie an abstract idea or other judicial exception to a field of use or to use with computers/networks, without meaningful additional limitations, are insufficient to make the claim 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bilski v. Kappos — claims describing hedging in commodities/energy markets merely linked the concept to those markets without meaningful limits; Parker v. Flook — limiting a mathematical formula to petrochemical/oil-refining industries did not impose meaningful limits; buySAFE Inc. v. Google, Inc. — using a computer to receive/send information over a network simply attempted to limit an abstract idea to a computer environment.
